query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The accelerated coupled degradation of the multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature arises from a synergistic tribo‐oxidation mechanism: dynamic removal of the protective oxide film by sliding wear repeatedly exposes lamellar FCC/B2 phase boundaries as microgalvanic sites that accelerate local corrosion, while corrosion preferentially attacks and softens the less noble phase at these boundaries, feeding back to increase material removal by wear, yielding total degradation exceeding the sum of individual processes.
generation.material_initial_state: Polished multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with lamellar FCC/B2 microstructure, pre‐oxidized at test temperature to form an initial protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Simultaneous sliding wear and electrochemical corrosion at 500 °C in 3.5 wt % NaCl solution under 10 N normal load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed.
generation.conditions: Temperature 500 °C; normal load 10 N; sliding speed 0.1 m/s; electrolyte 3.5 wt % NaCl; fully immersed contact; ambient pressure.
generation.structural_mediator: Dynamic thickness and integrity of the surface oxide film at FCC/B2 phase boundaries and the density of these lamellar interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Wear disrupts and removes oxide film, exposing fresh FCC/B2 boundaries which act as microgalvanic cells that accelerate corrosion; localized corrosion attack softens the less noble phase at interfaces, increasing material removal by wear (positive feedback loop).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the sum of mass losses in separate wear‐only and corrosion‐only tests: total mass loss >100 % greater; wear volume +20 % relative to wear‐only; corrosion current density +200 % relative to corrosion‐only.
generation.baseline: Additive sum of mass loss, wear volume, and corrosion current density obtained in separate wear‐only and corrosion‐only tests under identical temperature, load, speed, and electrolyte conditions.
generation.boundary: Applies to lamellar eutectic HEAs tested under sliding loads 5–20 N, temperatures 400–600 °C, in chloride‐containing electrolytes. Not expected to hold for single‐phase alloys, nonchloride environments, or static immersion without mechanical action.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate. The direction of synergy is supported by tribocorrosion literature but exact magnitudes may vary ±50 %.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct three sets of tests on the same alloy: (1) wear‐only (dry sliding) at 500 °C; (2) corrosion‐only (immersion) at 500 °C in 3.5 % NaCl open circuit; (3) simultaneous sliding wear plus electrochemical corrosion under identical load, speed, and electrolyte. Measure mass loss, wear volume, electrochemical current density, and friction coefficient.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the total mass loss in simultaneous wear‐corrosion tests is less than or equal to the sum of wear‐only and corrosion‐only mass losses AND neither the wear volume nor the corrosion current density increases by the predicted margins (wear ≤ +20 %; current density ≤ +200 %), the hypothesis is falsified.
